claims.claim: EPA defines environmental justice as the fair treatment and meaningful involvement of all people regardless of race, color, national origin, or income with respect to the development, implementation, and enforcement of environmental laws, regulations, and policies.

EPA defines 'fair treatment' as meaning no group of people should bear a disproportionate burden of environmental harms and risks, including those from industrial, governmental, and commercial operations or policies.

EPA defines 'meaningful involvement' to include that potentially affected community members have an appropriate opportunity to participate in decisions about activities that may affect their environment or health, and that decision-makers seek out and facilitate that involvement.

In 1982, North Carolina placed a landfill for PCB-contaminated soil in the majority-Black community of Afton in Warren County; residents and allies staged weeks of civil-disobedience protests that led to more than 500 arrests, and the episode is widely credited as a catalyst of the U.S. environmental justice movement.

In 1987 the United Church of Christ Commission for Racial Justice published Toxic Wastes and Race in the United States, which found that race was the strongest predictor of the location of commercial hazardous-waste facilities in the United States.

Benjamin Chavis, who directed the UCC Commission for Racial Justice that produced the 1987 report, is credited with coining the term 'environmental racism' in the early 1980s, defining it as racial discrimination in the targeting of minority communities for polluting facilities together with their exclusion from environmental decision-making.

Sociologist Robert Bullard, often called a father of environmental justice, documented these patterns in research including his 1990 book Dumping in Dixie, linking hazardous-facility siting to historical patterns of segregation.

The First National People of Color Environmental Leadership Summit convened in Washington, D.C., beginning October 24, 1991, drew delegates from all 50 states and beyond, and adopted the 17 Principles of Environmental Justice.

President Bill Clinton signed Executive Order 12898 on February 11, 1994 (published at 59 FR 7629), directing each federal agency to make achieving environmental justice part of its mission by identifying and addressing disproportionately high and adverse human health or environmental effects of its programs, policies, and activities on minority populations and low-income populations, and establishing an interagency working group chaired by the EPA Administrator.

EPA's EJScreen was the agency's primary environmental justice screening and mapping tool, combining environmental and demographic indicators; EPA removed it from its website in early 2025, and a mirror copy has been made available by outside groups.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact year Benjamin Chavis coined 'environmental racism'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says 'the early 1980s' and attributes the term to Chavis without asserting a single disputed year.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether environmental disparities reflect deliberate targeting or the outcome of market and land-use forces
positions: Some analyses emphasize housing markets, land prices, and pre-existing settlement patterns
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the documented disparities and both causal explanations, and notes this is an active area of research and policy rather than adjudicating cause.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic placeholder text ('Environmental Justice is a foundational concept... a simple way to apply it') with no substantive factual claims about the field, its definition, or its history.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced placeholder boilerplate with the EPA definition and documented history.
Added the fair-treatment/meaningful-involvement (distributive/procedural) structure absent from the draft.
Added dated, sourced historical anchors (1982, 1987, 1990, 1991, 1994) and the modern-tool/policy-status context (EJScreen, 2025).
rightsIssues: UCC report and UNC exhibition are copyrighted; used as REFERENCE_ONLY with facts synthesized and attributed, no extended wording reproduced.
Federal sources (EPA lexicon, EO 12898, EPA summary) are U.S. government works in the public domain; short EPA definitional phrasing is attributed.

sourceRecords.title: We Birthed the Movement: The Warren County PCB Landfill Protests, 1978-1982
sourceRecords.provider: University of North Carolina University Libraries
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebSearch summary of the UNC exhibition and corroborating results (NCpedia, scholarly review). Supports: 1978 illegal roadside PCB dumping; the 1982 state decision to site a PCB landfill in the majority-Black community of Afton, Warren County; weeks of civil-disobedience protests and more than 500 arrests; and the episode's status as a widely cited catalyst of the U.S. environmental justice movement. Also supports Robert Bullard's role in documenting siting patterns. Copyrighted exhibition; facts synthesized, no wording reproduced.
